# Sample Size for Two Independent Means {#sec-two-means}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Specify the mean difference and anticipated variability.
- Calculate a balanced normal-approximation sample size.
:::

## The idea

For a simple two-arm independent-groups comparison, define the expected between-group mean difference $\Delta$, the outcome SD, significance level, target power and allocation. Under a common SD and equal group sizes, a normal planning approximation has $n\approx2\sigma^2(Z_{1-\alpha/2}+Z_{1-\beta})^2/\Delta^2$ **per group**. Different-SD and unequal allocation formulations should use their corresponding variance expressions.

## When and how to apply it

The unit of the mean difference is the unit of the clinical measurement. The SD is not an arbitrary nuisance value; uncertainty in SD materially changes sample size. Normal-planning calculations are not exact Welch or Student t-based power methods.

## Formula at a glance

$$
n_{per\;group}\approx\frac{2\sigma^2(Z_{1-\alpha/2}+Z_{1-\beta})^2}{\Delta^2}
$$


## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
Consider 100 versus 105 mmHg with anticipated common SD 15 mmHg, two-sided $\alpha=0.05$ and 80% power. Substitute $\Delta=5$ and $\sigma=15$ in the balanced formula; use the calculator to verify the selected method.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Calculation logic

The example uses the stated planning assumptions and mathematical approximation. Explain why they apply before reporting the numerical result.

### Copy-and-run R

```r
sd <- 15; delta <- 5; za <- qnorm(.975); zb <- qnorm(.80)
ceiling(2 * sd^2 * (za + zb)^2 / delta^2)
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
Entering a pooled SD in a formula assuming equal variances does not establish that equal variances are realistic.
:::
